note: The unit test resets its bookkeeping and then continues to exercise the bitreader with attacker-controlled callback data.

code: static FLAC__bool read_callback(FLAC__byte buffer[], size_t *bytes, void *data)
note: The test harness supplies bytes from its input source through this callback into the library reader.
A sequence of bit-level reads is performed on the same input stream, forcing the reader to advance through internal buffer state.

code: end = br->words*FLAC__BYTES_PER_WORD + br->bytes + (uint32_t)bytes; br->words = end / FLAC__BYTES_PER_WORD; br->bytes = end % FLAC__BYTES_PER_WORD;
note: Read data is accumulated into a partially filled tail word, so the buffer can end with an incomplete word that later gets shifted and reused.
When previously consumed words are compacted, the implementation preserves a partial tail word and shifts the live buffer contents toward the front.

code: for(start = br->words; start < end; start++) br->buffer[start] = SWAP_BE_WORD_TO_HOST(br->buffer[start]);
note: On little-endian hosts the code byte-swaps every newly read word, including a tail word that may straddle the current logical end of stream.

code: const brword word = br->buffer[br->consumed_words]; if(bits < FLAC__BITS_PER_WORD) { *val = (FLAC__uint32)(word >> (FLAC__BITS_PER_WORD-bits)); }
note: Subsequent reads consume the shifted/swapped buffered word by indexing the current consumed word without any explicit bounds check.
If the internal word accounting is stale relative to the unread byte count, this dereference reads past the valid buffered data, producing the out-of-bounds read described in the vulnerability.
